content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper exploits the relationship among face components (i.e., eyes, nose, etc) to learn discriminative representation for kinship recognition. The relationship is further used as guidance for contrastive learning. Improved performance is reported in the FIW dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper is well written and easy to understand;
- The components guided contrastive learning and kinship recognition make sense, and SOTA performance is reported in the largest kinship recognition FIW dataset.

Weakness:
- The biggest concern is that the proposed method only evaluated and compared on a single dataset. To make the results more convincing, more datasets should be used for evaluation.
- The motivation is to use facial components for learning better representation, as the different facial areas illustrated in Fig.1.  But it is unclear how this assumption/motivation is being actually implemented in Fig.2, as the attention map could be any area of face image, and how can you make sure the model focus on key facial areas (i.e., eyes, nose, mouth), especially for the unaligned image pair?
- Several equation definitions are not  very clear. For example, what does it mean “i-th location of the j-region” in Eq-(1)?  What is F_{i}^{a}? Only positive pairs in Eq-(6)? 
- Please justify why the global sum pooling of attention map can be used as  the similarity value in Eq-(8)?
- It will be good to illustrate the different components for kinship verification, especially for the more challenging tasks, such as face makeup, pose, covering, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well written, with several equations needing a little bit more details.
The novelty of this paper is limited, as all the main components have been widely used in the literature.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is only evaluated on a single dataset, the novelty is limited, and also unclear whether the attention map will behave consistently with the claimed facial components.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new algorithm called FaCoRNet (Facial Componential Relation Network) for kinship recognition to determine whether the subjects in two facial images are kin or not. The results presented on a large FIW dataset looks promising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The use of face components (location/shape of eyes, mouth, nose etc) for learning relevance is an interesting idea.
- The comparative experimental results show that FaCorNet + Rel-Guide algorithm outperforms remaining state of the art algorithms in almost all combinations (BB/SS/SIBS etc)

Weaknesses:
- It is unclear how the facial components were extracted? Were they manually marked or did you use some existing algorithm  for segmenting the components? How robust is the component extraction in challenging conditions such as facial poses, illumination conditions, complex expressions, presence of facial hair etc?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper presents a novel FaCorNet algorithm that is backed by convincing results. The paper is also well written with good flow and organization of the sections in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I would recommend a strong accept.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new deep-learning approach for kinship based on two novel components. First, a tailored attention-based module incorporating "cross-relation between face images" to the learned representation. Second, a modified supervised contrastive objective, which adapts temperature according to the attention weights of this first module. Temperature is no longer a hyperparameter but is dependent on cross-attention weights between two samples, the lower these are the greater the gradient becomes, to focus the training on these samples. Equipped with these two additions, authors show SOTA performance on the largest public dataset for kinship classification.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The paper is well-written and organized making it easy to follow. 
- The authors highlight the contributions of their work.
- Related work is detailed and seems exhaustive, though I'm not an expert in the field of kinship classification.  
- Comparison to prior work is performed on a large and publicly available benchmark
- There is a good explanation of the experimental setting and code is provided. 
- Even though the authors introduce multiple new components, they provide an ablation study with respect to all their components.

Weakness:
- From reading the manuscript it's not entirely clear that kinship labels are used to constitute pairs and thus that the objective a supervised. 
- I believe the benchmark dataset is not properly cited. The authors cite "Survey on the analysis and modeling of visual kinship:
A decade in the making" (Robinson et al 2022) instead of "Families in the Wild (FIW): Large-Scale Kinship Image Database and Benchmarks" (Robinson et al 2016). 
- Experiments are not provided with confidence intervals suggesting there were run on a single seed. This absence of confidence intervals doesn't allow any conclusion on the statistical significance of the authors' method's superiority. Particularly here where the Zhang et al 2021 method is quite close. It would also be very helpful in the ablation study to properly assess each component's contribution. 
- In the ablation study, the main improvements are provided by CI, which is surprising, but this is never discussed.
- The authors limited their study to a single dataset. Even though it's the largest, it would be beneficial to verify similar conclusions on other benchmarks such as Family 101.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow and the contributions clearly highlighted. To the best of my knowledge, both the use of a cross-attention-based module for kinship recognition and a learnable temperature parameter for CL based on attention weights are novel ideas. The paper is mostly clear. However, experiments are run on a single dataset without any confidence intervals, given the relative closeness of the different methods in terms of accuracy, I don't believe one can conclude regarding the significance of the improvement over prior work as the authors do.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In this work, the authors propose an original deep-learning method relying on two clearly identified components. Their work is clearly presented and their method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the largest kinship recognition benchmark. However, the lack of confidence intervals and other datasets in their experiments weakness the authors' claim to achieve a significant improvement over prior works. It also makes unclear the magnitude of each component's contribution to this improvement. 

If the authors can address this concern, I will gladly increase my score.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:

+ The paper is well written and easy to read.
+ A Face Componential Relation Network (FaCoRNet) is introduced to learn discriminative kinship relation information between face components.
+ Experiments on FIW benchmark outperforms baseline methods.
 
Weaknesses:
- The novelty of this paper is limited, as many existing work has been proposed to use the relation information between face components in face / kiship recognition.
- The experimental evaluation is not sufficiant. This paper only evaluates the proposed FaCoRNet on FIW benchmark.
- Relation-Guided Contrastive Loss aims to estimate the similarity value, and its contribution is limited.
- There are typos in formulations (6), (7) and (8).

+ The Clarity and Quality of this work is good.
+ The novelty and originality of this work is limited.

content.title: Kinship Representation Learning with Face Componential Relation
content.abstract: Kinship recognition aims to determine whether the subjects in two facial images are kin or non-kin, which is an emerging and challenging problem. However, most previous methods focus on heuristic designs without considering the spatial correlation between face images. In this paper, we aim to learn discriminative kinship representations embedded with the relation information between face components (e.g., eyes, nose, etc.). To achieve this goal, we propose the Face Componential Relation Network (FaCoRNet), which learns the relationship between face components among images with a cross-attention mechanism, which automatically learns the important facial regions for kinship recognition. Moreover, we propose Relation-Guided Contrastive Learning, which adapts the loss function by the guidance from cross-attention to learn more discriminative feature representations. The proposed FaCoRNet outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by large margins for the largest public kinship recognition FIW benchmark. The code will be publicly released upon acceptance.
